title: Evolution Fine-Tuning: Learning to Discover Across 371 Optimization Tasks
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Fine-tuning on evolutionary trajectories improves search and learning, and lets one model combine strategies from diverse domains.
layout: 2 panels, left bar chart and right line plot, mascot icons, curved arrows
description: Two panels with pill-shaped titles. The left panel is a bar chart of Erdős minimum overlap, where lower is better. A grey Base LLM bar (0.495) is the zero-shot baseline. An arrow leads to a Finch bird box that points to the fine-tuned bars. Bars are grouped into Test-Time Search (OpenEvolve vs. EFT) and Test-Time Learning (TTT-Discover vs. EFT + TTT-Discover), on peach and orange shaded backgrounds. The EFT bars are lowest, with values around 0.381. The right panel is a step plot of best-so-far score against evolution iteration. A red Finch-9B curve climbs in steps and a dashed grey Qwen3.5-9B baseline stalls at 55%. Dark brown callout boxes name the strategies from other domains that drive each jump, with curved black arrows linking them to the curve. Bird mascots are used throughout.
caption: (Left) Evolution Fine-Tuning (EFT) serves as “mid-training”, boosting ℱinch’s discovery capability on the Erdős minimum overlap problem under both test-time search and learning. (Right) On NP-hard competitive programming (CALICO, UC Berkeley contest), EFT enables cross-discovery transfer: ℱinch solves problems by combining strategies acquired from diverse domains, such as combinatorial optimization, recommender systems, robust statistics/computer vision, and numerical optimization. In contrast, the base model without EFT relies on a single, repetitive strategy.
abstract: Would experience designing faster GPU kernels also help close in on a long-standing open mathematical conjecture? Large Language Models (LLMs) integrated into evolutionary search have recently produced state-of-the-art solutions on optimization tasks, including open mathematical conjectures, GPU kernel design, scientific law discovery, and combinatorial puzzles. To achieve this, prior work applied search scaffolds to one target task at a time, so every new problem is approached from scratch and the experience accumulated during search is discarded once the model finishes its attempt. This leaves the capability of iteratively evolving a solution (e.g., knowing which part to mutate and how, deciding when to backtrack) entirely in the scaffold rather than in the model itself. Whether the model itself could acquire this capability and reuse it across different tasks has been largely unexamined. To address this, we introduce Evolution Fine-Tuning (EFT), a mid-training paradigm that teaches LLMs to evolve solutions across tasks by converting evolutionary search trajectories into supervision. We construct Finch Collection, a 156K-trajectory dataset spanning 10 domains and 371 optimization tasks, and fine-tune open-source LLMs from 2B to 9B parameters. Empirically, EFT confers cross-task generalization: across 22 held-out tasks, our models surpass their base counterparts by 10.22% on average. Furthermore, when paired with test-time RL, our model matches state-of-the-art performance on two circle-packing tasks and outperforms its base-model counterpart on the ErdÅs minimum-overlap problem. EFT thus serves as a "practice phase" for general-purpose discovery agents that do not solve new problems from scratch.
